extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism / English literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted standards and critical principles for judging epic poetry and dramatic writing (Aristotelian unity, subject, style, moral responsibility), plus editorial practice for publishing readers' letters. Drawn from Addison/Steele commentary on Milton, Dryden, Rymer, Rapin, and theatrical morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable / Unified Action (Aristotelian requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fable ought to be dramatically constructed ... and that it should have for its Subject one entire and perfect action, having a beginning, a middle, and an end; forming a complete whole, like an animal, and therein differing ... from History.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's Poetics requires a single, complete action (unity of plot) for imitation by narration; this unity distinguishes poetry from history. (Quoted and discussed in footnote: Poetics III; see also references to unity and magnitude of tragedy vs epic.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and Magnitude (Tragedy vs Epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle ranked a perfect tragedy above a perfect epic; all the parts of the epic poem are to be found in tragedy, not all those of tragedy in the epic poem. There is less unity in epic imitation; any epic will furnish matter for several tragedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic must strive (as far as possible) to approach the imitation of a single action; the critic should evaluate degree of unity and whether subordinate parts possess their own magnitude without destroying the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic Subject and Heroic Requirements (Dryden's test)
rubrics_metrics.description: As for Mr. Milton ... his Subject, is not that of an Heroick Poem, properly so call'd: His Design is the Losing of our Happiness; his Event is not prosperous, like that of all other Epique Works ... His Heavenly Machines are many, and his Human Persons are but two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden's criteria for an 'heroic' epic: (a) subject should be a proper heroic subject (often the fortunes of a hero), (b) event should be prosperous (successful outcome), (c) an epic normally treats one principal person; many 'heavenly machines' and few human persons count against Milton on this traditional measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form / Rhyme vs Blank Verse (Dryden on style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither will I justify Milton for his Blank Verse, tho I may excuse him ... For whatever Causes he alledges for the abolishing of Rhime ... his own particular Reason is plainly this, that Rhime was not his Talent; he had neither the Ease of doing it, nor the Graces of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden defends poetic form rules (rhyme) as a conventional test of talent; deviation (blank verse) can be excused only if shown to be a conscious necessity or superior talent. Critics should note the poet's reasons and talents when judging formal choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthodoxy of Critical Rules (Rapin/Rymer on Aristotle as rule-source)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no arriving at Perfection but by these Rules, and they certainly go astray that take a different course.... And if a Poem made by these Rules fails of success, the fault lies not in the Art, but in the Artist; all who have writ of this Art, have followed no other Idea but that of Aristotle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapin/Rymer assert that following Aristotelian rules is necessary for poetic perfection; critics who hold this view treat Aristotle as the authoritative rulebook and measure works by conformity to those precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic must have a principal person/subject (Gildon's objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is plain that the proposition of all the heroic poems of the ancients mentions some one person as the subject of their poem... But Milton begins his poem of things, and not of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gildon's standard: an epic should centre on one person (a hero). Deviation into a 'poem of things' (broad, cosmological scope) is viewed as a departure from the epic form and grounds for critique under traditional metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical Flexibility — classical rules can be exceeded (Addison's stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison ... resolved to meet [the classical critics] on its own ground ... and do battle ... he might suggest ... that even the Divine Aristotle sometimes fell short of perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison's position is that while Aristotle's rules are valuable, they are not absolute; critics should allow for exceptions where genius or new species (e.g., Milton's 'divine' epic) justifies departure from strict classical norms. Evaluate both technical conformity and poetical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility of the Author / Limits of Wit on Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: It is so mean a Thing to gratify a loose Age with a scandalous Representation of what is reputable among Men, not to say what is sacred, that no Beauty, no Excellence in an Author ought to atone for it ... Wit should be tried by this Rule, and an Audience should rise against such a Scene, as throws down the Reputation of any thing which the Consideration of Religion or Decency should preserve from Contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and dramatists are judged not only for wit and art but for moral effect: deliberately promoting vice or scandalising sacred/reputable institutions is condemnable regardless of artistic merit. Audiences and critics should resist applauding immoral depiction simply because it is cleverly executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and Character-appropriateness in Dramatic Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir Roger and his Mistress are Monsters of the Poets own forming; the Sentiments in both of them are such as do not arise in Fools of their Education ... This very one Character of Sir Roger ... has done more towards the Disparagement of Holy Orders, and consequently of Virtue it self, than all the Wit that Author or any other could make up for ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be plausible and consistent with their social position and education. Unnatural or exaggerated portrayals that misrepresent classes or institutions (e.g., clergy) are a serious failing and ethically harmful, regardless of the author's wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial practice for publishing correspondents' letters
rubrics_metrics.description: I am of Opinion that I ought sometimes to lay before the World the plain Letters of my Correspondents in the artless Dress in which they hastily send them, that the Reader may see I am not Accuser and Judge my self, but that the Indictment is properly and fairly laid, before I proceed against the Criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should publish letters in original, 'artless' form sometimes to demonstrate fairness and that criticism is grounded in readers' own words; when altering letters, change language only 'if it can be done without Prejudice to the Sense' and omit inessential compliments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical criteria for a good marriage (social/moral standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing but the good Qualities of the Person beloved can be a Foundation for a Love of Judgment and Discretion ... Whoever expects Happiness from any Thing but Virtue, Wisdom, Good-humour, and a Similitude of Manners, will find themselves widely mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This social-moral rule prescribes virtues to seek in a spouse (virtue, wisdom, good-humour, similar manners, prudence, frugality), and criticises seeking riches or display as foundations for marital happiness. Useful as a behavioural/evaluative standard in social commentary.
